# Visualisation with `ggplot2` {#sec-m1-ggplot2}

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(stringr)
library(readxl)

colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2",
             "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem",
             "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino",
             "tku")

cabotagem <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-"))
stopifnot(ncol(cabotagem) == length(colunas))
names(cabotagem) <- colunas

cabotagem <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), str_squish)) |>
  dplyr::filter(tku > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(uf_origem  = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_origem),
         uf_destino = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_destino),
         tku_bi     = tku / 1e9)
```

## The grammar

Every `ggplot2` chart has three mandatory parts:

1. **data**: a `data.frame`;
2. **aesthetic mapping** (`aes`): which column goes to the x axis, y axis, colour, size;
3. **geometry** (`geom_*`): how the data are drawn.

```{r}
#| label: fig-primeiro
#| fig-cap: "Minimal structure of a chart"
por_uf <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = uf_destino) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi))

ggplot(por_uf, aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) +
  geom_col()
```

Layers are added with `+`. From there everything is refinement: scales, labels, theme.

## The geometries you will use

### Bars

```{r}
#| label: fig-barras
#| fig-cap: "Coastal shipping TKU by destination state (2025)"
ggplot(por_uf, aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::number(tku_bi, accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    title = "Coastal shipping: TKU by destination state",
    subtitle = "Billions of tonne-kilometres, 2025",
    x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: ANTAQ, Estatístico Aquaviário."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Note two technical choices: **horizontal** bars (long names stay readable) and
`reorder()` (orders by value, not alphabetically). Use `geom_col()` when the height is in a
column of the data, and `geom_bar()` when you want `ggplot2` to count the rows.

### Grouped and stacked bars

```{r}
#| label: fig-barras-perfil
#| fig-cap: "Composition of TKU by cargo profile"
por_perfil <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(uf_destino, perfil)) |>
  dplyr::filter(uf_destino %in% por_uf$uf_destino[1:8])

ggplot(por_perfil, aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi), fill = perfil)) +
  geom_col() +                                 # stacked (default)
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL, fill = "Cargo profile") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Switching to proportions, with `position = "fill"`, the chart now reads as composition:

```{r}
#| label: fig-barras-fill
#| fig-cap: "Share of each cargo profile in destination TKU"
ggplot(por_perfil, aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi), fill = perfil)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", direction = -1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

`position = "dodge"` puts the bars side by side.

### Scatter plot

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Number of links versus total TKU by destination state"
resumo_uf <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(ligacoes = dplyr::n(), tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = uf_destino)

ggplot(resumo_uf, aes(x = ligacoes, y = tku_bi)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7, colour = "#1a5b8a") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = uf_destino), size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.5,
              colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Number of OD links", y = "TKU (billion t·km)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

### Histogram, density and cumulative distribution

For very skewed variables, such as TKU, the logarithmic axis is the difference between an
unreadable chart and an informative one.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of TKU per OD link (log scale)"
ggplot(cabotagem, aes(x = tku)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#1a5b8a", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = "TKU per link (t·km, log scale)", y = "Number of links") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dens-cdf
#| fig-cap: "Density (left) and cumulative distribution (right)"
g1 <- ggplot(cabotagem, aes(x = tku)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#1a5b8a", alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "TKU (log)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

g2 <- ggplot(cabotagem, aes(x = tku)) +
  stat_ecdf(geom = "step", linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#1a5b8a") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(x = "TKU (log)", y = "Cumulative links") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

patchwork::wrap_plots(g1, g2)
```

The cumulative curve directly answers a planning question: *how many pairs
concentrate what fraction of the TKU?*

### Boxplot

```{r}
#| label: fig-box
#| fig-cap: "TKU per link, by cargo profile"
ggplot(cabotagem, aes(x = tku, y = reorder(perfil, tku, FUN = median))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.4, fill = "grey95") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = "TKU per link (log)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

### Lines: time series

```{r}
#| label: fig-linha
#| fig-cap: "Example time series with made-up data"
serie <- data.frame(
  ano = 2015:2025,
  tku_bi = c(24.1, 23.4, 25.8, 27.2, 28.9, 27.1, 30.4, 32.2, 33.8, 35.1, 36.4)
)

ggplot(serie, aes(x = ano, y = tku_bi)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = "#1a5b8a") +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = "#1a5b8a") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2025, 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "TKU (billion t·km)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## Scales, labels and formats

The `scales` package handles number formatting. Its defaults follow the English convention
(decimal point, comma for thousands); for reports in Portuguese, the Brazilian convention is the
opposite, and the arguments `big.mark` and `decimal.mark` switch it:

```{r}
scales::number(1234567.891, big.mark = ",", accuracy = 0.01)                       # English
scales::number(1234567.891, big.mark = ".", decimal.mark = ",", accuracy = 0.01)   # Brazilian
scales::percent(0.1234, accuracy = 0.1)
scales::label_number(scale = 1e-9, suffix = " bn")(8332538649)
scales::comma(1234567)
```

Applying it to the axis:

```{r}
#| label: fig-escalas
#| fig-cap: "Axis with formatted numbers"
ggplot(por_uf |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 8), aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 0.1)
  ) +
  labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Other useful scales:

```{r}
#| eval: false
scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 40))                    # limits
scale_y_continuous(transform = "log10")                      # transformation
scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b/%Y", date_breaks = "3 months")  # dates
scale_fill_viridis_c()                                   # continuous, perceptually uniform
scale_fill_viridis_d()                                   # discrete
scale_colour_manual(values = c("Rodoviário" = "#1a5b8a", "Cabotagem" = "#e07b39"))
coord_flip()                                             # swaps the axes
coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10))                         # crops without dropping data
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`scale_x_continuous(limits = ...)` **removes** the observations outside the limit (and affects means and
smoothers); `coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)` only zooms. To crop the view, use
`coord_cartesian()`.
:::

## Factors: controlling the order

```{r}
#| label: fig-forcats
#| fig-cap: "Explicit order of the categories"
cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = perfil) |>
  dplyr::mutate(perfil = forcats::fct_reorder(perfil, tku_bi)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tku_bi, y = perfil)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") +
  labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

`forcats` functions worth memorising: `fct_reorder()` (orders by another variable),
`fct_infreq()` (by frequency), `fct_rev()` (reverses), `fct_lump_n()` (groups the small
categories into "Other") and `fct_relevel()` (manual order).

```{r}
cabotagem |>
  dplyr::mutate(sh2_top = forcats::fct_lump_n(sh2, n = 5, w = tku)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = sh2_top) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi))
```

## Panels (`facet`)

```{r}
#| label: fig-facet
#| fig-cap: "One panel per cargo profile"
cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(perfil, uf_destino)) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(tku_bi, n = 5, by = perfil) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") +
  facet_wrap(~perfil, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

`scales = "free"` gives each panel its own scale: good for comparing **shape**,
bad for comparing **magnitude**. Choose deliberately.

## Annotations

```{r}
#| label: fig-anotacao
#| fig-cap: "Highlighting a specific point"
maior <- cabotagem |> dplyr::slice_max(tku, n = 1)

ggplot(resumo_uf, aes(x = ligacoes, y = tku_bi)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(data = resumo_uf |> dplyr::filter(uf_destino == maior$uf_destino),
             colour = "#e07b39", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 30, y = max(resumo_uf$tku_bi) * 0.95,
           label = stringr::str_glue("Largest link: {maior$cidade_origem} > {maior$cidade_destino}"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(resumo_uf$tku_bi), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "OD links", y = "TKU (billion t·km)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## Themes and visual identity

```{r}
#| eval: false
theme_minimal(); theme_bw(); theme_classic(); theme_void()
```

To standardise every chart in a report, define the theme once:

```{r}
tema_mt <- function(base_size = 11) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.15)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"),
      plot.caption  = element_text(colour = "grey45", size = rel(0.8)),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position  = "bottom"
    )
}

theme_set(tema_mt())
```

From here on, every chart in the document inherits this theme.

## 2D frequency maps

When many points overlap (typical of GPS coordinates or OD pairs),
two-dimensional histograms show density instead of stacked points.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bin2d
#| fig-cap: "Density of links by TKU band and number of links of the state"
cabotagem |>
  dplyr::left_join(resumo_uf |> dplyr::select(uf_destino, ligacoes), by = "uf_destino") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ligacoes, y = tku)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 20) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "Links of the destination state", y = "TKU of the link (log)", fill = "Number of\nlinks") +
  tema_mt()
```

`geom_hex()` does the same with hexagonal cells (requires the `hexbin` package). In module 2 this
same logic appears over geographic space, with hexagon grids.

## Class breaks: Jenks and alternatives

When classifying values into bands (the mandatory step of any thematic map), the
break method completely changes how the result reads.

```{r}
library(classInt)

valores <- resumo_uf$tku_bi

quebras_jenks  <- classInt::classIntervals(valores, n = 5, style = "jenks")
quebras_quant  <- classInt::classIntervals(valores, n = 5, style = "quantile")
quebras_iguais <- classInt::classIntervals(valores, n = 5, style = "equal")

round(quebras_jenks$brks, 2)
round(quebras_quant$brks, 2)
round(quebras_iguais$brks, 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-jenks
#| fig-cap: "The same states classified by three break methods"
classificar <- function(x, estilo) {
  q <- classInt::classIntervals(x, n = 5, style = estilo)
  cut(x, breaks = q$brks, include.lowest = TRUE, dig.lab = 2)
}

resumo_uf |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Jenks      = classificar(tku_bi, "jenks"),
    Quantile   = classificar(tku_bi, "quantile"),
    `Equal intervals` = classificar(tku_bi, "equal")
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(Jenks, Quantile, `Equal intervals`),
                      names_to = "metodo", values_to = "classe") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = 1, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi), fill = as.integer(classe))) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~metodo) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", breaks = 1:5) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Class") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

| Method | When to use |
|:--|:--|
| `jenks` (natural breaks) | skewed data; maximises the difference between classes |
| `quantile` | guarantees the same number of units per class; good for rankings |
| `equal` | bands of equal width; good when the scale has its own meaning |
| `pretty` | round breaks, readable in a legend |
| `fisher` | equivalent to Jenks, faster on large datasets |

::: {.callout-note}
Keep this block: in module 5 it comes back applied to choropleth maps with `sf`, and the
choice of method will be justified in the final report.
:::

## Saving charts

```{r}
#| eval: false
g <- ggplot(por_uf, aes(tku_bi, reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) + geom_col()

ggsave("resultados/tku_uf.png", g, width = 18, height = 12, units = "cm", dpi = 300)
ggsave("resultados/tku_uf.pdf", g, width = 18, height = 12, units = "cm")  # vector
ggsave("resultados/tku_uf.svg", g, width = 18, height = 12, units = "cm")  # editable
```

For institutional reports, prefer **PDF or SVG**: the chart does not lose quality when
enlarged or printed. Set the dimensions in centimetres, thinking of the usable width of the
page (about 16 cm on A4 with standard margins).
